data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The conflict dissolves if we view corroboration as a measure of informational content rather than truth likelihood; we prefer high-content theories because they teach us more, regardless of their truth.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If scientists actually care about truth, not just information.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If a false high-content theory leads to dead ends more often than a low-content true one.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'information' implicitly relies on the stability of the world (induction).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is 'informational maximization'. Corroborated theories have high empirical content (they risk more). Even if false, a highly corroborated theory provides more structure and potential for further error elimination than a trivially true or untested one. We prefer them not because they are likely true (induction) nor because they are definitely true (verisimilitude), but because they are the most informative tools for generating new problems and tests. The cost is abandoning the goal of 'truth' for the goal of 'progress'.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
